newsitem.title: CHINA: North Korean children face widespread famine.
newsitem.headline: North Korean children face widespread famine.

text.p: Communist North Korea's rigid control of foreign access to its famine victims is masking the extent of the catastrophe gripping the country, international food relief workers said on Monday.
"You are never unattended. You have to negotiate every image. You just don't have free access," said Dave Toycen, head of the Canadian division of the World Vision aid group.
Toycen, who returned on Sunday from a four-day trip to North Korea, said signs of widespread famine were everywhere.
"You see people all over the countryside picking grasses," he said. "They're always picking something to eat. That's quite obvious all through the countryside."
He said there had been more access to famine regions in recent months and attributed this to North Korea accepting the extent of the crisis and the need for urgent international food relief.
The North Korean government must decide whether it is going to "save face or save lives", Toycen said.
World Vision was one of the first relief groups to bring the Somali and Ethiopian famines to international attention and it has worked extensively in Bosnia.

Describing one scene, Toycen said: "There was someone, 11 or 12 years old, and he was just a walking ghost. I mean he was extremely malnourished. That was the most extreme case I saw but I saw many other children who were clearly malnourished."
Watt Santatiwat, who accompanied Toycen, said strict control of foreign aid groups and Western journalists made it difficult to show the world what was happening in North Korea.

"Our delegation was not allowed to see areas of the country where starvation is worst. So we cannot show you or our donors pictures and video that document the harsh realities of the extent of the suffering," he said.

A report by World Vision doctor Milton Amanyun estimated 30 percent of the children he examined during a July visit suffered from severe malnutrition and another 30 percent from moderate malnutrition.
Amanyun examined children aged two and under at a series of children centres through the country.
International relief groups have estimated that a searing drought this year wiped out nearly three-quarters of the North Korean maize crop and raised the spectre of starving children.

"Aid agencies must have access. It's a situation they (the North Koreans) have never faced before. If foreign governments and North Korea can't get together, then it will be the politics of adults that kills the children of North Korea," Toycen said.
